About me

Learning humans is a lifelong project.

I love learning how people think and behave. Though not trained psychologically, the number of years I've spent on Earth and interacting with fellow humans has taught me one thing: humans are complicated — and that's exactly what keeps me learning.

2015 was the year I took a leap of faith, going on sabbatical to study UX design with General Assembly. From then, my perspective on service design changed. I learnt to see things not just as "nice" design, but how people actually interact with a service or product — online and offline.

My goal: building experiences that make work, communication, and technology feel a little more seamless and a lot more human.

Empathy plays a huge role in me and my eyes and mind began to widen.

Case Study 04

Leading Change Management

GIC's intranet ran on ageing technology with outdated security. As the company grew across nine offices, staff felt further from top management and had few ways to take part. The new platform had to give staff a voice and bring leadership closer, and it would only work if 1,500 people actually changed how they used it.

This is the intranet project from Case Study 1, told through a change lens.

Duration

6–8 months to first launch · about 1.5 years end to end across both phases

Organisation

GIC, Singapore's sovereign wealth fund

Framework

ADKAR: Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement

Reach

1,500 employees · 9 global offices

Teams

Technology, Corporate Communications, external vendors & office champions

The 30-second version

Motion summary · Directed with AI · How I made it

Awareness
Desire
Knowledge
Ability
Reinforcement

Awareness · Why change

Old security, a growing workforce, and a gap at the top.

Three things made the case for change. The intranet's security was out of date. Headcount was growing across our nine offices. And staff had little real interaction with top management, so leadership felt distant. We wanted a platform that kept staff informed and gave them a voice.

We built awareness before launch with teasers and email announcements. Office champions carried the message in each office, so it didn't land as just another headquarters memo.

📣 Teasers ✉️ Email announcements 🙋 Office champions
Awareness
Desire
Knowledge
Ability
Reinforcement

Desire · Winning buy-in

The people with the most to lose.

The strongest pushback came from content managers. Some had to relearn how they published. For others, publishing was new work on top of their existing jobs. Simply telling them to adopt it was never going to work.

What changed their minds

  • We showed them the audience data the new platform could give them: what staff read, how long they stayed and what they reacted to.
  • With that insight, they could pick the right way to reach their audience instead of guessing. The extra effort now came with something useful in return.
Awareness
Desire
Knowledge
Ability
Reinforcement

Knowledge · Equipping publishers

Training first, then guides to fall back on.

We ran training for content managers and produced guides they could come back to afterwards, so nobody had to remember everything from a single session.

Awareness
Desire
Knowledge
Ability
Reinforcement

Ability · Making it easy

A lite version first, then the full platform.

  • 1
    Designed with the people who'd use itWe interviewed 30 staff across three personas, including content managers, whose one requirement was that the system be intuitive. Five rounds of user testing came before launch.
  • 2
    Rolled out in two phasesPhase one launched a lite version so staff could get used to it. Phase two brought the full platform once the habit had formed.
  • 3
    Built around the original problemBlogs and Yammer let staff hear directly from management, and comments and reactions let them respond. That closed the gap that had started the project.
Awareness
Desire
Knowledge
Ability
Reinforcement

Reinforcement · Making it stick

We kept listening after launch.

Feedback kept coming in on how the intranet could fit people's work better. Investment professionals, for example, rarely had time to read on a laptop. So we built a mobile-lite version they could read on the go. We changed the platform to fit their day instead of asking them to change their habits.

37%
Bounce rate, down from 59%
2.2min
Article read time, up from 1.8 min
20%
More engagement: likes and comments on articles and announcements
2.3%
Increase in viewership

Looking back

The hardest part wasn't building the platform. It was the content managers, who had every reason to see it as extra work. Showing them what was in it for them did more than any instruction from above.

AI-Directed Work

AI-Directed Motion

Some stories land better when you can watch them. I use AI like a production team: I shape the story, set the constraints and make the editorial calls, and Claude builds it, entirely in code.

Role

Concept, scriptwriting & creative direction

Made with

Claude (AI): animation, typography and original synthesized music, all in code. No stock footage or design software.

Output

Two 30-second films · 1080p

My approach

  • 1
    DistilCut the source down to one clear story and decide what each scene must say.
  • 2
    DirectBrief the visual metaphors, style and constraints, the way I'd brief a design agency.
  • 3
    EditReview every cut as a viewer would and send it back until it reads well.

Turning Research into Motion

A dense study on prayer, meditation and the brain, made watchable.

Film 02 · Turning Research into Motion

The Neuroscience of a Quiet Mind

Research too dense to read, so I made it watchable.

Strategy
Discovery
Analysis
Design
Production

The spark

A research study on how prayer and meditation affect the brain was fascinating but dense, and I caught myself skimming. It covered blood flow, metabolism, pain relief, the amygdala, emotions and neuroplasticity, all in nested bullet points and clinical terms. I wondered how many readers would stop halfway, and whether motion could carry the same ideas more easily.

Strategy
Discovery
Analysis
Design
Production

Distilling the study

I cut the research down to a simple three-act story a viewer could follow without pausing.

I · The body II · The heart III · The wiring
Strategy
Discovery
Analysis
Design
Production

One visual metaphor per idea

  • 1
    Pain reliefA jagged incoming signal that smooths into a calm wave.
  • 2
    The amygdalaA red alarm pulse that slows down and cools to blue.
  • 3
    Calmer heartA heartbeat trace that visibly slows as stress words are struck out.
  • 4
    NeuroplasticityOld pathways fading while new gold ones light up and strengthen.
Strategy
Discovery
Analysis
Design
Production

The film

Sound on · 30 seconds

Iterating for the viewer

The first cut ran 15 seconds. It looked great, but the text disappeared before I could finish reading it, which defeated the whole point. I had it retimed to 30 seconds so each idea holds long enough to land, while the transitions keep their energy.

2×
Runtime, retimed for readability
0
Stock footage or design software

What I learned

Turning research into motion is an exercise in editing: what to cut, what to show instead of say, and how long a viewer needs before you move on. AI made the production possible for one person, but the storytelling and judgement calls were still mine.
